## Critics of the multiverse {#the-multiverse-has-its-critics .smaller}

::: {.small}
- "Robustness is better assessed with a **few thoughtful models** than with billions of regressions" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; answering @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources] – only *justified* models targeting the *same estimand* belong in one curve. This workshop's curve keeps only the specifications that a review of every option judged justifiable for the claim, and setting each option beside its twins does the job that every critic endorses: it locates where the argument must happen
- "**There is only one correct analysis**" once the question is fully specified [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne] – your preregistered specification guards against *cherry-picking*, and their deeper point is that preregistering a choice does not yet make it *justified*, which is what the estimand and DAG work were for
- "What's a multiverse **good for** anyway?" – reflection, persuasion, or inference, and each purpose needs a *differently built* universe [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood]. The full menu serves **reflection** and the curve of the claim moves towards **persuasion**; how much more to read into it is the open debate
:::

::: {.src}
The book-length how-to: @YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational; the estimand diagnosis of the red-card study: @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
The method that you have practised is the subject of a live debate. Katrin Auspurg, who with Josef Brüderl traced the spread in the red-card study to teams that answered different questions, replied to a study of about three point six billion estimates that only thoughtful and justified models belong in a curve, and the curve of this workshop keeps only the options of the menu that were judged justifiable answers to the claim. Lakens and colleagues argue that once the question is fixed only one analysis implements it correctly, and their point that preregistering a choice does not make it justified is why the causal graph comes before the preregistration. Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask whether a multiverse is meant for reflection, persuasion or inference, each of which needs a differently built set; the full menu serves reflection, and the curve, with a published reason for every option, moves towards persuasion. [advance]
:::

## The one-correct-analysis argument {#there-is-only-one-correct-analysis .smaller}

::: {.small}
The argument from Lakens and colleagues runs in four steps:

- A research question, **fully specified**, implies a quantity to be estimated
- That quantity, together with the design and the assumptions you are willing to make, implies **one analysis** that estimates it
- So a spread of results is not evidence of legitimate diversity. It is evidence that **most of those specifications are wrong** – they estimate something else
- On this reading, showing a wide curve is closer to an admission than to a robustness check
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Take it back to the red cards. Twenty-nine teams modelled one count of red cards as **linear, logistic or Poisson**. Those are claims about how the outcome was generated, and they cannot all be right – so on this argument most of the spread is error.
:::

::: {.src}
@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne
:::

::: notes
The strongest objection to the multiverse comes from Lakens and colleagues, and it deserves to be stated at full strength. A research question, once fully specified, implies a quantity to be estimated, and that quantity, together with the design and the assumptions that you are prepared to make, implies one analysis that estimates it. It follows that a spread of results is evidence that most of the specifications are wrong, because they estimate something other than the quantity that you said you wanted, and not evidence of legitimate diversity. On that reading, a wide specification curve comes closer to an admission that the question was never specified than to a robustness check. [advance] Applied to the red-card study, a linear, a logistic and a Poisson model of one count of red cards are three claims about how the outcome was generated, which cannot all be right. I find the argument uncomfortable, and I think that it is largely right.
:::

## Identifying the one correct analysis {#how-would-you-know .smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Grant the argument, and suppose that **one correct analysis exists**. Which one is it?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Getting there needs the estimand *and* the identification assumptions *and* agreement about the measurement – and reasonable people can disagree about each of the three.
:::

::: {.fragment}
So the curve complements the one-correct-analysis view: it is a **map of the disagreement that remains**, drawn because we cannot yet settle it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
And it points at what to argue about: the **few decisions that move the estimate**.
:::
::::

::: notes
Suppose, then, that one correct analysis does exist. The next question is which one it is, and how you would know. Reaching it needs the estimand, the assumptions of identification and agreement about how the construct is measured, and reasonable people can disagree about each of the three, as you found in the tasks. I therefore read the curve as a companion to the view that there is one correct analysis, a map of the disagreement that remains, drawn because we cannot yet settle it. Read in this way, the curve shows where the disagreement lies, in the few decisions that move the estimate, and on our claim we have already found the one that matters most. Arguments about those decisions are arguments about the claim itself, and they belong in the paper rather than in a footnote on robustness.
:::

## What preregistration settles {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does settle**

- That your specification was not chosen *because of* the result
- That your rule for what counts as support was fixed before you had a result
- That a reader can see what you intended, and what you changed
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does not settle**

- Whether the specification was **any good**
- Whether it estimates the quantity that your question implies
- Whether the assumptions behind it hold

A badly reasoned analysis that is preregistered is still badly reasoned; the preregistration only adds a timestamp
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
That is why the estimand and the DAG came **first** today: preregistration protects a choice, and the causal reasoning is what justifies it.
:::

::: notes
Preregistration settles a specific and limited set of things, and both columns matter. It settles that your specification was not chosen because of the result that it gave, that your rule for what counts as support was fixed before you had a result, and that a reader can see what you intended and what you changed afterwards, guarantees that no other practice provides. It does not settle whether the specification was any good, whether it estimates the quantity implied by your question, or whether its assumptions hold, so that a badly reasoned analysis that is preregistered is still badly reasoned. [advance] That is why we worked on the estimand and the graph first, since preregistration protects a choice, while the causal reasoning is what justifies it.
:::

## Exploration and preregistration {#you-are-analyst-no.-6-for-real-this-time .smaller}

::: {.big}
- Aim 2: assess the **robustness** of the constrained result
:::

::: {.small}
  - **In Task 4** you explored: several specifications, tried in order to find out what they do. That was the right way to learn them

  - **In Task 5** you preregister **one** specification: it goes into the preregistration block of your report *before* it runs, with a reason that your DAG supports

  - **The code is identical.** The difference is that one of these can be chosen because of its result and the other cannot
:::

::: notes
Earlier you reproduced the constrained result of one analyst of the robustness study, and in Task 4 you explored several specifications, tried in whatever order interested you, in order to find out what they do, which was the right way to learn them. In Task 5 you preregister one specification: it goes into the preregistration block of your report before it runs, with a reason supported by your causal graph. The code of the two activities is identical, and the difference is that a specification explored in Task 4 can be chosen because of its result while the one preregistered in Task 5 cannot, a difference that very few published papers state.
:::
